```{webr}
library(tidyverse)
theme_set(theme_gray(base_size = 14))
survey <- read_csv("data/sleep_survey.csv") |>
  mutate(early_class = if_else(has_early_class == "Yes", 1, 0))  # 1 = has an early class
```
:::


## Where we left off

::: {.callout-important title="Recall from last class"}
We added structure to a linear model (i.e. categories, several predictors).
:::

Last class ended with a question: *how do we know a model works on data it has not seen?*

:::{.callout-caution title="Today's Agenda:"}

- split our data into a **training set** and a **test set**
- measure how well a model predicts, against a simple *baseline*
- predict a binary outcome with **logistic regression**

:::

## Motivation: Studying

::: {.callout-caution title="How do you prepare for an exam?"}
Suppose that a resourceful student got their hands on last year's exam, they memorized all of the answers word-for-word. Do you think if they would do well on a **new** exam?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="A model can do the same"}
Basically it fit the data it learned from very closely (like past exam questions), and there is a possibility that it still miss on **new** cases (new exam questions).
:::

To find out whether the model is good, we need to test the model on data it has **never seen**.


## What is predictive modelling?

Models do different jobs:

- Descriptive: summarize a pattern in the data
- Inferential: test a claim about the world
- **Predictive:** estimate values for cases we have **not observed**

::: {.callout-note title="Today's goal"}
Predict the outcome for a **new** student. What matters is not how well the model fits the students we already have, but how well it does on the next ones.
:::


# Look before you model

## The outcome


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-18_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


Roughly bell-shaped and centred in the low 70s, with a few unusual grades at either end.


## A checklist before modelling

::: {.callout-caution title="Before you fit anything, ask"}
1. What does the outcome look like? Is it skewed or oddly shaped?
2. Are there unusual values in the outcome or the predictors?
3. Do any predictors overlap a lot (multicollinearity)?
4. How do the predictors relate to the outcome?
:::

Exploring first is what tells you which modelling choices make sense.


# Spending our data

## Training set and test set {.smaller}

We have a limited amount of data, so we split it in two.

| | Training set | Test set |
|---|-----|-----|
| **What it is** | The data we use to **build** the model | Data we put aside for later|
| **Used for** | Fitting the model | Checking how well it predicts **new** cases |
| **How often** | As many times as we like | Once at the end |

## The basic rule 

::: {.callout-tip title="A common split: 80% / 20%"}
Put about **80%** of the data in the training set and about **20%** in the test set, chosen **at random**.
:::

- Too little training data: the model learns poorly
- Too little test data: the score is unreliable
- There is no perfect ratio, and 80/20 is a sensible default


## Example: splitting the survey


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(18)   # makes the random split reproducible

n <- nrow(survey)
train_rows <- sample(n, size = round(0.8 * n))

train <- survey[train_rows, ]    # 80% of students
test  <- survey[-train_rows, ]   # the other 20%

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
train  test 
  240    60 
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note title="What does set.seed() do?"}
The split is random every time you run the code, but `set.seed()` makes it so that it repeats the **same** random choice every time, so everyone with the same seed gets the same answer.
:::

## Fancier splits (out of scope)

::: {.callout-note title="You know what? You can do more than this, but it is out of scope"}
- **Stratified splits:** keep the mix of groups (or outcome values) the same in both sets
- **Time-based splits:** train on the past, test on the most recent data
- **Validation sets and resampling:** a third set, or repeated splits, for choosing between models
- **Grouped data:** keep all rows from one person or unit together
:::

If you're curious, read [Tidy Modeling with R, Chapter 5](https://www.tmwr.org/splitting).


# Predicting a grade

## The baseline: guess the average

The simplest "model" gives every student the average grade of the training set.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
baseline <- mean(train$avg_grade)
baseline
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 72.90917
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-important title="A model has to beat the baseline"}
If a model cannot do better than guessing the average, then it is not worth using.
:::

## Measuring the error

For each student, the **error** is the gap between the actual grade and the prediction.

::: {.callout-note title="Root mean squared error (RMSE)"}
It is a statistical tool that we use to measure the "typical size of an error", in the same units as the outcome (grade points). A model with smaller RMSE is better.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
rmse <- function(actual, predicted) sqrt(mean((actual - predicted)^2))
```
:::


The baseline's typical error is about the standard deviation of the grades.

## Three models

Recall from last time, we used `lm()` to formulate our linear regression model.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 1. Simple: study hours and program
fit_simple <- lm(avg_grade ~ study_hours_week + program, data = train)

# 2. Flexible: everything, plus interactions with program
fit_flex <- lm(
  avg_grade ~ (study_hours_week + sleep_hours + sleep_quality +
               stress_level + num_courses + work_hours_week) * program +
              favourite_drink + has_early_class,
  data = train
)
```
:::


The flexible model has many more coefficients, so it can bend itself closely around the training data.

## Errors on the training data


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
train_error <- tibble(
  model = c("Baseline standard deviation", "Study hours + program", "Everything + interactions"),
  train_error = c(
    rmse(train$avg_grade, baseline),
    rmse(train$avg_grade, fitted(fit_simple)),
    rmse(train$avg_grade, fitted(fit_flex))
  )
)
train_error
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  model                       train_error
  <chr>                             <dbl>
1 Baseline standard deviation        9.17
2 Study hours + program              4.75
3 Everything + interactions          4.39
```


:::
:::



## Now the test set


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
results <- train_error |>
  mutate(test_error = c(
    rmse(test$avg_grade, baseline),
    rmse(test$avg_grade, predict(fit_simple, test)),
    rmse(test$avg_grade, predict(fit_flex, test))
  ))
results
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 3 × 3
  model                       train_error test_error
  <chr>                             <dbl>      <dbl>
1 Baseline standard deviation        9.17       9.79
2 Study hours + program              4.75       5.77
3 Everything + interactions          4.39       6.16
```


:::
:::



## Training vs. test error


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
results |>
  pivot_longer(c(train_error, test_error), names_to = "set", values_to = "error") |>
  mutate(set = str_remove(set, "_error"), model = fct_inorder(model)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = model, y = error, fill = set)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_x_discrete(guide = guide_axis(n.dodge = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Typical miss (grade points)", fill = NULL)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-18_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::


## What do we see?

- The baseline scores about the same on both sets: it learned almost nothing
- Adding study hours and program helps a lot
- A more flexible model always fits its training data a little better. The question is whether that carries over to the test set

::: {.callout-important title="Overfitting"}
A model that follows the quirks of its training data too closely, and then does worse on new data. Training error alone cannot show it.
:::



# Predicting binary variables

## A yes/no outcome

So far the outcome has been a number. What if the question is yes or no? For example: can I predict whether a student has an early class in the morning?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
train |>
  count(has_early_class) |>
  mutate(share = n / sum(n))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 2 × 3
  has_early_class     n share
  <chr>           <int> <dbl>
1 No                134 0.558
2 Yes               106 0.442
```


:::
:::


`early_class` is **1** for yes and **0** for no. Roughly six in ten students have no early class, so our baseline is to **always guess "No"**.

## Why not a straight line?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ggplot(train, aes(x = sleep_hours, y = early_class)) +
  geom_jitter(height = 0.03, alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = FALSE, color = "firebrick") +
  geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = "binomial"), se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "Sleep (hours per night)", y = "Has an early class (1 = yes)")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](DATA100-F26-Lecture-18_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=672}
:::
:::



## Logistic regression {.smaller}

::: {.callout-note title="Logistic regression"}
A model for a binary outcome. The `glm()` is like `lm()` with `family = binomial` says the outcome is yes/no. We are going to skip the inference for logistic regression in this course. The interpretation for the coefficients are very different. Take ST494 if you are interested :D
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
logit_fit <- glm(early_class ~ sleep_hours, data = train, family = binomial)
summary(logit_fit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

Call:
glm(formula = early_class ~ sleep_hours, family = binomial, data = train)

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)   6.8225     1.1848   5.758 8.51e-09 ***
sleep_hours  -1.0738     0.1805  -5.948 2.71e-09 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 329.44  on 239  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 282.20  on 238  degrees of freedom
AIC: 286.2

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4
```


:::
:::


## From probabilities to predictions


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
test_results <- test |>
  mutate(
    probability = predict(logit_fit, test, type = "response"),
    predicted   = if_else(probability > 0.5, 1, 0)
  )

test_results |>
  select(sleep_hours, probability, predicted, early_class) |>
  head(6)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
# A tibble: 6 × 4
  sleep_hours probability predicted early_class
        <dbl>       <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>
1         4.6       0.868         1           1
2         5         0.811         1           1
3         5.8       0.644         1           1
4         7.1       0.310         0           0
5         6.2       0.541         1           0
6         7.8       0.175         0           0
```


:::
:::



To get a yes or no, pick a **cutoff**. A common choice is **0.5**: predict yes when the probability is above it.

## Model Accuracy


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(test_results$predicted == test_results$early_class)   # model accuracy
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.6666667
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
table(actual = test_results$early_class, predicted = test_results$predicted)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
      predicted
actual  0  1
     0 32 12
     1  8  8
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note title="Accuracy"}
The share of predictions that are correct. The table counts correct and incorrect predictions for each actual answer.
:::



## Exercise {.smaller}

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it yourself
1. Split `survey` 80/20 with a seed of your choice.
2. Fit a logistic model for `early_class` using `sleep_hours` and `stress_level` on the training set.
3. Compute the test accuracy, and compare it with always guessing "No".
4. Change the seed and run it again. Does the accuracy change?
:::


::: {.cell exercise='logistic_split'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: logistic_split

set.seed(...)
n <- nrow(survey)
train_rows <- sample(n, size = round(0.8 * n))
train <- survey[train_rows, ]
test  <- survey[-train_rows, ]

fit <- glm(early_class ~ ..., data = train, family = binomial)

prob <- predict(fit, test, type = "response")
pred <- if_else(prob > 0.5, 1, 0)

mean(pred == test$early_class)    # model accuracy
```
:::



::: {.cell exercise='logistic_split' solution='true'}
```{webr}
#| exercise: logistic_split
#| solution: true

set.seed(18)
n <- nrow(survey)
train_rows <- sample(n, size = round(0.8 * n))
train <- survey[train_rows, ]
test  <- survey[-train_rows, ]

fit <- glm(early_class ~ sleep_hours + stress_level, data = train, family = binomial)

prob <- predict(fit, test, type = "response")
pred <- if_else(prob > 0.5, 1, 0)

mean(pred == test$early_class)    # model accuracy

```
:::


## More than two categories

What if the outcome has **several** categories, such as `program`?

- One idea: fit one yes/no model per program ("is it Arts or not?"), then pick the program with the **highest probability**
- `multinom()` does this in one step, and the probabilities across programs add up to 1


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(nnet)

program_fit <- multinom(program ~ avg_grade + study_hours_week,
                        data = train, trace = FALSE)

program_pred <- predict(program_fit, test)   # predicted program for each test student
```
:::


## Can I guess someone's program?


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
mean(program_pred == test$program)     # accuracy
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0.7833333
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
table(actual = test$program, predicted = program_pred)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
             predicted
actual        Arts Business Engineering Health Sci Science
  Arts          11        0           0          0       0
  Business       2        9           0          0       0
  Engineering    0        0           9          5       0
  Health Sci     1        0           2          7       0
  Science        0        2           0          1      11
```


:::
:::



::: {.callout-caution title="A slightly artificial question"}
In real life we would rarely predict a student's program from their grade. It is just a convenient example of more than two categories.
:::


## Summary

- Predictive modelling cares about new data, not just the data we have
- Training set builds the model; test set validates it.  
- A flexible model can look great on training data and overfit
- Logistic regression predicts a probability for a binary outcome
